new_en: Which forms of melacha a non-Jew may perform for a Jew. It contains 6 seifim: A person may contract with a non-Jew for a melacha and fix a price, and the non-Jew performs it for his own benefit. Even though he performs it on Shabbos, it is permitted. When does this apply? When it is done privately, so that it is not generally recognized that the melacha being performed on Shabbos belongs to a Jew. But if it is known and public, it is forbidden, because one who sees the non-Jew engaged in it does not know that a fixed price was agreed upon, and will say that so-and-so hired the non-Jew to perform melacha for him on Shabbos. Therefore, one who contracts with a non-Jew to build his courtyard or wall, or to harvest his field, if the melacha is within the city or within the techum, he may not allow the non-Jew to perform the melacha for him on Shabbos because of observers, who do not know that a fixed price was agreed upon. {Rama: Even if he lives among non-Jews, there is concern for guests who come there, or for members of his household, who may suspect him. [Beit Yosef in the name of the responsa of the Ashkenazim]} If the melacha is outside the techum, and there is also no other city within the techum of the place where the melacha is being performed, it is permitted. Regarding a non-Jew who brought a Jew's sheep into a pen in his field, see above, siman 537, seif 14.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama restored in source order and cross-reference restored.

new_en: A woman may go out with a knot made as a remedy against the evil eye, so that it should not prevail; with absorbent material tied and secured in her ear; with absorbent material in her sandal when it is tied to the sandal; and with a sandal or shoe that is closed on all sides, even if the material is not tied. She may also go out with absorbent material that she prepared for her menstrual flow. {Rama: This is so that blood should not fall upon her and cause her distress. [Beit Yosef in the name of the authorities]} Even if it is not tied, it is permitted, since it is repulsive and there is no concern that she will remove it and carry it. She may likewise go out with pepper or a grain of salt, or anything placed in her mouth as a remedy, provided that she did not place it in her mouth initially on Shabbos. If it fell out, she may not return it to her mouth. A false tooth or a gold tooth may be worn outside according to some authorities, while others prohibit it.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; repaired cut post-Rama material.

new_en: One who borrows an item from another should not say to him, 'Lend it to me,' using a term that implies a long-term loan, because there is concern that he may write it down. Rather, he should say, 'Let me borrow it.' In a foreign language in which there is no distinction between the expressions for lending and borrowing, he should say, 'Give it to me.' {Rama: If he borrows on Shabbos and the lender does not wish to trust him, he may leave collateral with him, but he should not say, 'Here is collateral,' because that resembles a weekday transaction. [Beit Yosef in the name of Orchot Chaim] Just as one does not borrow in the manner of a loan on Shabbos, so too one does not repay on Shabbos. [Rosh, siman 115]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: It is forbidden to say to a non-Jew on Shabbos, 'Take this meat and cook it for yourself,' even if the Jew is not responsible for providing his food. {Rama: It is permitted, however, to tell him to perform melacha for himself. [Hagahot Mordechai, chapter 5; Ramban, Parashat Bo]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: Any rabbinic shevut is permitted during bein hashmashot for the sake of a mitzvah, for example, to tell a non-Jew to light a lamp for him during bein hashmashot, or, if he was preoccupied and needs to tithe, to tithe during bein hashmashot. {Rama: Anything that one is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do on Shabbos may likewise not be told to him before Shabbos if he will perform it on Shabbos, except in cases expressly permitted above. One may not tell a non-Jew on Shabbos to do after Shabbos something that may not be done on Shabbos, unless the matter can be described in a manner that does not constitute a direct instruction to perform forbidden melacha.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; rebuilt from complete source case.

new_en: If one took a fruit in his hand to eat it, recited the blessing over it, and it fell from his hand and was lost or became repulsive, he must recite the blessing again, even though more of the same species was before him when he blessed over the first one. {Rama: This applies only when he did not have in mind to eat the other fruit. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 4; Kol Bo; Agur; Abudarham; Responsa Maharil, siman 92]} He must say, 'Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever,' because he uttered the Divine Name in vain. If, when the fruit fell, he had already said, 'Blessed are You, Hashem,' but had not yet said 'our God,' he should conclude, 'teach me Your statutes,' so that it appears that he is reciting a verse and he has not uttered the Divine Name in vain. But one who stands beside a flowing water channel recites a blessing and drinks, even though the water he drinks was not before him when he recited the blessing, because that was his intention from the outset. {Rama: See above, seif 1, regarding the law when one recited a blessing in error.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; both Rama glosses restored.

new_en: If a Jew and a non-Jew are partners in an animal, the non-Jew may perform melacha with it on Shabbos if, at the outset when they acquire it, the Jew stipulates with the non-Jew that the non-Jew will take its use on Shabbos and the Jew on a weekday. If they did not stipulate at the outset, it is forbidden even if they stipulate afterward. If the Jew lends the animal to the non-Jew as a complete loan, so that the non-Jew has the authority to remove it if he wishes without the Jew's permission, the price is charged to the non-Jew, and responsibility for the animals rests upon the non-Jew, it is permitted. Some permit it even where the non-Jew does not have authority to remove them, provided that the price is charged to the non-Jew as a debt and the non-Jew then designates them as an apotiki to the Jew, meaning that payment will be collected only from these animals, or pledges them to him as collateral, provided that he does not say that the transfer takes effect 'from now.' Some also permit it if the Jew warns the non-Jew not to perform melacha with the animal on Shabbos, and stipulates that if he transgresses and does so, responsibility for it, even for unavoidable accidents, will rest upon the non-Jew, and this is recorded in their courts. In that event, when the non-Jew performs melacha with it on Shabbos it is not regarded as the Jew's animal, because the non-Jew has acquired responsibility for its unavoidable loss. {Rama: All these avenues of permission are accepted halacha, and one may use whichever of them he wishes. Even if the animal belongs entirely to the Jew, its law is as though it were jointly owned with the non-Jew, provided that he publicizes that he arranged the matter in a permitted manner.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; complete cut text restored.

new_en: If merchandise is in danger of being ruined on Shabbos by rain or something else, or if a flood of water, meaning a stream or accumulation of water, is coming and will cause him monetary loss, or a barrel of wine has become damaged and its contents are being lost, it is permitted to call a non-Jew even though he certainly knows that the non-Jew will save the property. Regarding covering merchandise, fruit, or another item because of rain, see above, siman 338, seif 7. It is likewise permitted to say to a non-Jew, 'Whoever saves it will not lose,' just as in the case of a fire they permitted saying, 'Whoever extinguishes will not lose.' There is an authority who says that this was permitted specifically in the case of a fire. See also simanim 334, 305, and 336, seif 9.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; all cross-references restored.

new_en: If one sold merchandise to another before the Moed, there is an authority who forbids demanding its payment during the Moed unless the purchaser is a person who is not usually found in the seller's locale and happened to be there during Chol HaMoed, so that failure to collect would constitute a potential loss. It appears to me, however, that since the seller converted the money due into a debt before the Moed, it is regarded as a loan, and he may collect it during Chol HaMoed even from a person who is ordinarily found in the seller's locale. {Rama: It is likewise permitted to bring a legal claim regarding debts that one is permitted to demand. [Mordechai, end of the chapter Mi SheHafach] One may also take the necessary steps to preserve such a claim when delay may cause a loss.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: It is permitted to write documents of kiddushin, documents recording pledged marriage contributions, gittin, receipts, deathbed dispositions, gifts, prozbul documents, appraisal documents, and support documents. A document of pledged contributions records that a person undertakes to give his son or daughter a specified amount. A deathbed disposition is a document stating that this shall stand and take effect. A prozbul is an enactment for the lender so that he will not lose his money, thereby enabling the borrower to find someone willing to lend to him. Appraisal documents record that beit din appraised a borrower's property and gave it to the creditor. A support document records that beit din sold land to provide sustenance for a wife and daughters and recorded the act of beit din, or alternatively records one who undertook to support his wife's daughter. It is also permitted to write documents of chalitzah and mi'un, arbitration documents, and judicial rulings. {Rama: It is permitted to write a ketubah during the Moed [Kol Bo], although some prohibit it [Semak].} A letter of greeting that a person sends to his fellow may be written, even concerning merchandise that is not in danger of loss; some prohibit writing greetings. [Tur in the name of Halakhot Gedolot] The custom is to be stringent even regarding our ordinary cursive writing.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; complete definitions and post-Rama material restored.

new_en: A householder's clothes press, meaning a device used to press garments after laundering, consisting of two boards one above the other with the garments between them, may be opened in order to take garments from it for Shabbos. A craftsman's press is forbidden, because it is fastened tightly and opening it resembles dismantling.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: The law of chametz found in a Jew's shop where the workers are non-Jews, or the reverse. It contains 1 seif: If the shop belongs to a Jew and its stock, meaning the merchandise and shop utensils, belongs to a Jew, while the workers who enter it are non-Jews, chametz found there after Pesach is forbidden for benefit. If the shop belongs to a non-Jew and its stock belongs to a non-Jew, while the workers who enter it are Jews, chametz found there is permitted even for eating. This is the textual reading of Rashi and Rabbeinu Hai; Rabbeinu Chananel has the reverse reading.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: Not to place the lamps near the doorway on Friday night. It contains 2 seifim: On Friday night one must place some barrier outside, between the lamps and the doorway, because of the wind, so that the lamps will not be extinguished when he opens the door.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew.

new_en: The order of Hoshana Rabbah. It contains 11 seifim: On the seventh day, which is Hoshana Rabbah, the custom is to increase the recitation of psalms as on Yom Tov. {Rama: We do not recite Nishmat, but we do recite Mizmor LeTodah, Ein Kamocha, and Shema Yisrael as on Yom Tov. The Kaddish after Mussaf is recited in the Yom Tov melody. The custom is not to perform weekday melacha until after leaving the synagogue. When there is a circumcision on Hoshana Rabbah, the piyyut Zechor Berit is recited, before Ana Azon Chen. The early authorities wrote that there is an omen in the shadow of the moon on the night of Hoshana Rabbah regarding what may happen to a person or his relatives during that year. Some write that one should not examine this carefully, so that his fortune should not be impaired, and also because many do not understand the matter properly. It is better to be wholehearted and not investigate the future; so it appears to me.} We increase the candles somewhat, as on Yom Kippur. {Rama: Those who are meticulous customarily immerse themselves before dawn, as on the eve of Yom Kippur [Minhagim], and some customarily wear a kittel as on Yom Kippur.} This is because on the Festival judgment is rendered concerning water. The custom is to loosen the binding of the lulav. We circle seven times and recite many supplications concerning water.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; two Rama glosses separated and restored to source position.

new_en: The law of one who wishes to add requests to the blessings. It contains 4 seifim: If one wishes to add to any of the middle blessings a request corresponding to that blessing, he may add it. How so? If he has a sick person, he asks for mercy for him in the blessing Refa'einu; if he needs sustenance, he asks for it in Birkat HaShanim; and in Shomea Tefillah he may ask for all his needs, because that blessing encompasses all requests. {Rama: When he adds a request, he should first begin the blessing and only afterward add the request; he should not add the request before beginning the blessing. [Tur, siman 567]} According to Rabbeinu Yonah, when one adds a request corresponding to a blessing on behalf of all Israel, he should phrase it in the plural and not in the singular, and he should add it only at the end of the blessing, not in its middle. But if he asks for his own particular need, such as a sick person in his household or his own need for sustenance, he may ask even in the middle of the blessing, provided that he phrases it in the singular and not in the plural. In Shomea Tefillah, and likewise at the end of the prayer, whether before Yihyu LeRatzon or after it, he may ask in either singular or plural, whether for his own needs or for the needs of the community.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; legacy leaked text discarded.

new_en: Laws that apply between the Amidah and Yihyu LeRatzon. It contains 3 seifim: If one wishes to interrupt to answer Kaddish or Kedushah between the Amidah and Yihyu LeRatzon, he does not interrupt, because Yihyu LeRatzon is part of the prayer. But between Yihyu LeRatzon and the other supplications it is permitted. {Rama: This applies specifically in a place where the custom is to say Yihyu LeRatzon immediately after the prayer. But where the custom is to say supplications before Yihyu LeRatzon, one also interrupts for Kaddish and Kedushah. In these lands the custom is to interrupt during Elohai Netzor before Yihyu LeRatzon, and therefore one also interrupts there for Kedushah and Kaddish.} One who is accustomed to say supplications after his prayer may shorten them when necessary. If he has completed his prayer but has not yet stepped back, the laws governing interruption are as stated above.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama moved to source position and post-Rama material restored.

new_en: One who washes his hands for fruit is among the arrogant. {Rama: This applies specifically when he washes them as though there were a halachic obligation to do so. But if he washed them for cleanliness because his hands were not clean, it is permitted. [Hagahot Semak]} Regarding roasted meat, there is an authority whose words indicate that even though its juice is still moist upon it, its law is like fruit. A cooked dish of wheat kernels, when they are dry, likewise has the law of fruit.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; post-Rama clauses restored.

new_en: One who enters where three people have eaten. It contains 1 seif: If three ate and are reciting Birkat HaMazon, and a person who did not eat enters, if he enters when the leader says, 'Let us bless Him of whose food we have eaten,' he responds after him, 'Blessed and praised be His name always, forever and ever.' If he enters when the others are responding, 'Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten,' he answers Amen after them. {Rama: Likewise, for every blessing that a person hears, he is obligated to answer Amen. [Tur; Beit Yosef in the name of Halakhot Gedolot and Semag]} If they are 10, he says, 'Blessed is our God, and praised be His name always, forever and ever.' The same applies if he was present when they finished eating but did not eat with them; this is how he responds after the leader and after those answering.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; French legacy text discarded.

new_en: Kiddush must be recited in the place of the meal. Within one house, moving from one corner to another is considered the same place. If one recited Kiddush in one corner intending to eat there and then changed his mind and ate in another corner of the same house, even in a large hall, he need not recite Kiddush again. Some say that whenever he can see the place where he recited Kiddush, even from a house to a courtyard, he need not recite Kiddush again. Some also say that it is effective if one recites Kiddush in one place with the intention from the outset to eat in another place, provided both places are within one house, for example from room to room or from the roof to the ground floor. {Rama: From the house to the sukkah is considered a change of place. See also above, at the beginning of siman 178. The latter view is the primary one.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama normalized and restored in source position.

new_en: One may not go out on Shabbos with an amulet that is not established as effective. If it is established, one may go out with it. This applies whether the writer is established but the particular amulet is not, for example, he wrote one incantation on three separate amulets and all three healed three different people, in which case the writer is established for that incantation whenever he writes it, though not for other incantations, and a later amulet is not itself thereby established; or whether the amulet is established but the writer is not, for example, he wrote one incantation on one amulet and it healed three times, in which case that amulet is established for any person. All the more so, it applies when both the writer and the amulet are established, for example, he wrote one incantation on three amulets and each one benefited three people, or one person three times. The writer is then established for this incantation in every amulet he writes, and those amulets are established for every person. {Rama: This is specifically when the two established statuses arose together. But if the writer was already established and afterward he made an amulet that healed three times, we do not attribute those cures to the amulet's independent effectiveness, but to the expertise of the writer, who had already been established. [Hagahot Ashiri; this is also implied by Tosafot according to the explanation cited by Beit Yosef]} But if he wrote three amulets for one person and they healed him three times, neither the writer nor the amulet is thereby established. It is permitted to go out with an established amulet, whether it consists of writing or of medicinal roots, whether for a dangerously ill person or for one who is not dangerously ill. This is not limited to one who has already suffered an epileptic seizure and wears it as a remedy; even one who has not yet contracted the illness, but comes from a family prone to epilepsy and wears it so that the illness should not seize him, may do so. He may tie and untie it in the public domain. However, he may not attach it to a bracelet or ring and go out with it into the public domain, because people would then say that he is wearing it as an ornament, and that is forbidden because it is not an ornament.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; complete expert-writer and expert-amulet distinctions preserved.

new_en: All those species that we said are invalid because of the defects explained above, or because they were robbed or stolen, are invalid only on the first day of Yom Tov; on the other days, all are valid. {Rama: Some authorities invalidate a stolen lulav for all 7 days, and this is the custom. A borrowed lulav, however, fulfills the obligation. [Tur; Maggid Mishneh in the name of the authorities] On the other days it is permitted to take another person's lulav without his knowledge, because a person is pleased that a mitzvah be performed with his property, and it is regarded as borrowed. [Terumat HaDeshen, siman 100, and his rulings, siman 159] One should nevertheless return it to the place from which he took it.} Regarding defects arising from the species itself, the rules on the remaining days follow the distinctions stated by the authorities. In a place where two days of Yom Tov are observed, one may use on the second day species that are invalid only because of the first-day requirement, but should not recite a blessing over them when a valid set is available. If another person has a valid lulav and etrog, he should take the valid set with permission and recite the blessing over it.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; cut post-Rama continuation restored.

new_en: If there are many people reclining at the meal, the greatest among them breaks the bread. {Rama: If they are equal and one of them is a Kohen, it is a mitzvah to give him precedence. If the Kohen is an am ha'aretz and the other is a Torah scholar, the Torah scholar takes precedence. If the Kohen is also a Torah scholar but is of a lesser level than the other scholar, it is preferable to give the Kohen precedence, though there is no obligation to do so. See above, siman 201; Mordechai, chapter Bnei HaIr; and Beit Yosef, siman 135, in the name of Rashba.} If the host is among them, he breaks the bread even if the guest is greater. The one reciting the blessing should first say, 'With the permission of my teachers and masters.' [Or Zarua; Beit Yosef in the name of Shibbolei HaLeket]
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; host clause correctly placed after Rama and cross-reference restored.

new_en: If one puts on tefillin several times in one day, he must recite the blessing over them each time. If they slipped from their proper position and he handles them to return them to their place, he must recite the blessing. {Rama: If he is returning only one of them, he recites the blessing appropriate to one who puts on only one tefillah, as explained below in siman 26. [Rama's own ruling]} If he removed them with the intention of putting them back immediately, he must nevertheless recite the blessing again. If he was putting on the arm tefillin and had recited the blessing, and while tightening it the knot broke so that he must make another knot, if he did not divert his attention from the tefillin he need not recite another blessing. If the arm tefillin loosened before he put on the head tefillin, he tightens it and need not recite another blessing. But if he had already put on the head tefillin and afterward the arm tefillin loosened, he tightens it and recites the blessing. {Rama: Some say that he should not recite a blessing in this case [Tur, siman 8], and this is the prevalent custom, as was explained above in siman 8, seif 14.} One may recite the blessing over borrowed tefillin, but not over stolen tefillin.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; both Rama glosses placed in sequence.

new_en: If two prayer services are before him, one Minchah and one Mussaf, for example, he delayed Mussaf until 6 and a half seasonal hours, which is the time for Minchah, he should pray Minchah first and afterward Mussaf. {Rama: If, however, he prayed Mussaf first, he has fulfilled his obligation. [Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba]} Some say that this applies specifically when he presently needs to pray both, for example because he wishes to eat and may not eat until he has prayed Minchah. But if he does not presently need to pray Minchah, he may pray Mussaf first. Some say that in a congregation one should not pray Minchah before Mussaf, lest people err in the future. {Rama: When the time of Minchah Ketanah has arrived, however, Minchah may be prayed at that time. [Rosh in the name of the Yerushalmi]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; two Rama glosses separated.

new_en: An item concerning which there is no concern of trapping or of having been detached from the ground, but which was merely brought from outside the techum, if a non-Jew brought it for himself it is permitted even that same day. If he brought it for a Jew, it may be moved, but the Jew for whom it was brought may not eat it until after Shabbos, after the amount of time required to perform the act has elapsed. {Rama: Some say that the night is not included in this waiting period, and the required time is counted from Sunday morning. [Semak; Mordechai]} Other Jews may benefit from it on Shabbos itself. Some say that even the person for whom it was brought may benefit from it immediately after Shabbos. Even where moving the item is permitted, it may be moved only within 4 amot, unless it is in a city surrounded by a wall that was enclosed for residential purposes, meaning that it was inhabited first and enclosed afterward. Ordinarily, a city is presumed to have been enclosed for residential purposes, whereas a fortress is not. {Rama: See further in siman 401.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; restrictions after Rama restored.

new_en: The laws of a courtyard smaller than 4 amot and of a drain. It contains 3 seifim: A courtyard smaller than 4 by 4 amot that adjoins the public domain may not have water poured into it on Shabbos during the summer. Since it does not contain 4 amot, the 2 se'ah of water that a person ordinarily uses each day will not be absorbed there, and it is evident that he intends the water to flow out into the public domain. Therefore, one must make a pit or receptacle large enough to contain 2 se'ah within the courtyard, whether inside the house or outside it, so that the water will be absorbed there. {Rama: Even if the pit is outside the courtyard in the public domain, it is sufficient where it is covered in the manner explained by the authorities.} In the winter, when courtyards are ordinarily muddy and water runs through them in any event, there is greater room for leniency. The same principles govern a drain that carries water from private premises toward the public domain, according to whether the water first enters a place where it can be absorbed or collected before reaching the public domain. {Rama: The local construction and the manner in which the water ordinarily flows determine whether the arrangement is permitted.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; complete seif rebuilt with Rama material.

new_en: Five groups that spent Shabbos in a large hall and divided it with partitions: if they all pass through one another, because only the outermost section has an opening to the courtyard and all of them pass through it, only the two innermost groups must contribute to the eruv, while all the others are considered a gatehouse for them. If each group has an opening to the courtyard, {Rama: or if they do not pass through one another, but each has an opening to the gatehouse before it and the gatehouse opens to the courtyard [Beit Yosef],} then if the partitions reach to within 3 tefachim of the ceiling, so that each section is a room unto itself, even if the partitions are curtains, and the residents of the courtyard place their eruv in one of the other houses of the courtyard, each group in the hall must contribute to the eruv. But if they placed the eruv in this hall, none of them need contribute at all, because they all live in this house, and the house in which the eruv is placed need not contribute. Likewise, if there are no other residents in the courtyard, they do not require an eruv. If they divided the hall with partitions that do not reach the ceiling, even if the courtyard residents place their eruv in one of the other houses, one eruv suffices for all 5 groups. {Rama: If some made partitions and some did not, those who made partitions are considered separate, while those who did not are considered jointly situated. [Maggid Mishneh, chapter 4]} If they actually reside in upper stories, even if the residents of the courtyard placed the eruv in the hall, each group must contribute to the eruv. But one who has a tutor or a scribe in his house, and likewise students who study before a rabbi and live in his house, each in his own room, even if each has an opening to the courtyard and eats and sleeps in his room, do not prohibit carrying for the others.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: Further laws of the Seder. It contains 7 seifim: He washes his hands and recites the blessing over washing the hands. He takes the matzot in the order in which he placed them, the broken matzah between the 2 whole ones, holds them in his hand, and recites HaMotzi and the blessing over eating matzah. He then breaks from the upper whole matzah and from the broken one, from both together, and dips them in salt. {Rama: The custom is not to dip them in salt on the first night, because fine bread does not require salt.} He eats them together while reclining, a kezayit from each. If he cannot eat approximately 2 kezayitim together, he first eats the portion associated with HaMotzi and afterward the portion associated with the blessing over eating matzah. He then takes a kezayit of maror and immerses all of it in charoset, but does not leave it there, so that its bitter taste will not be nullified. For this reason he must shake the charoset off it. He recites the blessing over eating maror and eats it without reclining. He then takes the third matzah, breaks from it, wraps it together with the maror, and dips it in charoset. {Rama: Some say that it should not be dipped, and so it is stated in the customs, and this is what I have seen practiced.} He says, 'In remembrance of the Temple, according to Hillel,' and eats them together while reclining. From the time he recites the blessing over eating matzah, he should not interrupt with anything unrelated to the meal until he has eaten this sandwich, so that the blessing over eating matzah and the blessing over eating maror also apply to this sandwich.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The law of the blessings for the recitation of Shema and whether they require intention. It contains 5 seifim: The second blessing is Ahavat Olam. {Rama: Some say Ahavah Rabbah, and this is the custom throughout Ashkenaz.} It does not begin with Baruch because it follows directly after the blessing Yotzer Or. Regarding whether it exempts one from Birkat HaTorah, see above, siman 47.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: If the hole was a full thumb joint distant from the corner and threads of the woof tore away until the required measure no longer remained, it is valid, because the required measure was present when these tzitzis were attached. {Rama: The custom is to make a reinforced hem around the hole so that it will not tear there and become less than the required measure. For the same reason, a hem is also made along the lower edge of the garment. [Beit Yosef in the name of Semak and Kol Bo]} Some say that there is no required measure within the width of the garment, while others say that the law of the garment's width is the same as its length, and their words appear correct.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: Women and servants are exempt because tzitzis is a time-bound positive mitzvah. {Rama: Nevertheless, if they wish to wrap themselves in tzitzis and recite the blessing, they have permission to do so, as with other time-bound positive mitzvot. [Tosafos, Rosh, and Ran, chapter 2 of Rosh Hashana and chapter 1 of Kiddushin] However, it appears presumptuous, and therefore they should not wear tzitzis, since it is not an obligation incumbent upon the person. [Agur, siman 27] This means that a person is not obligated to purchase a tallis in order to become obligated in tzitzis. Below, in siman 19, the case discussed is one who already has a four-cornered garment and wears it.} A tumtum and an androgynos are obligated because of doubt and should wrap themselves without a blessing. A tumtum is one whose sex is unknown; an androgynos has both male and female sexual characteristics. {Rama: According to the custom that women recite blessings over time-bound positive mitzvot, they too should recite the blessing. [Rama's own ruling]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of moving a door, window, and lock on Shabbos. It contains 10 seifim: A window stopper, such as a board or anything else used to close a window, may be used to close it even if it is not tied, and we do not say that this constitutes adding to a building, provided that one designated it before Shabbos for closing the window. A reed that was prepared to be used as a bolt need not be tied to the door. Nevertheless, it resembles building more than a window stopper, and mere designation from the previous day is insufficient; it must be prepared for this purpose. According to Rashi, this means preparing it as a utensil fit for some use, such as turning olives or cracking nuts. According to Rabbeinu Tam, it need not be fit for another use; once one prepared it, performed an act upon it, and designated it for this purpose, that is sufficient. {Rama: Through this it is considered a kli shemelachto l'heter and may be moved, as explained above in siman 308, seif 2. [Beit Yosef and Rambam]} A door bolt that is a peg inserted into the threshold below resembles building even more, and the foregoing is insufficient. One may not lock with it unless it is tied. If it has a knob at its head, meaning that one end is thick and fit for pounding, so that it resembles a utensil, it is sufficient even if it is tied with a thin cord that is not fit to carry it, even if it is tied not to the door itself but to the door bar, and even if the cord is long and does not hang in the air at all but lies entirely on the ground. If it has no knob at its head, then if it is tied to the door itself, a thin cord that is not fit to carry it is sufficient, even if it lies entirely on the ground. If it is tied not to the door but to the bar, the knot must be strong enough for the peg to be carried by it. Even then it need not hang, and it is permitted even if it lies entirely on the ground, because it is forbidden only when one removes it and places it in a corner.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: A rear courtyard behind the houses that is not regularly used for entering and leaving: if one made a door for its opening, or hung a reed mat there, or fenced a breach with thorns in the form of a door, then if it has a hinge, meaning that the door is pierced and a pointed piece of wood is fixed into it so that it can be inserted into a socket and swing back and forth, or even if it has no hinge now but previously had one, it may be used to close the opening even if it drags on the ground, provided that it was tied and hung for use as a door. This is not considered building, because the fact that it had a hinge makes it recognizable as a door. {Rama: All the more so if it still has a hinge, provided that he does not return the hinge to its socket, as will be explained below in siman 519. [Beit Yosef]} But if it has no hinge and never had one, it may not be used to close the opening unless it is raised above the ground. An opening that is regularly used for entering and leaving may be closed with such a door even if it never had a hinge and it drags on the ground.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The law of repairing tefillin and the law of the straps. It contains 5 seifim: If the leather of 2 adjacent compartments of the head tefillin became damaged, if the tefillin are old they are invalid, and if they are new they are valid as long as the leather forming the base of the compartments remains intact. {Rama: The compartments themselves must also remain intact, except that they may be somewhat torn. [Beit Yosef] Some say the reverse, that old tefillin are valid and new tefillin are invalid. [Rashi and Rosh] It appears to me that one should be stringent and invalidate both.} What are considered new? As long as, if one were to pull them by the straps, the compartment would spread and open, it is called new. If it does not open, it is called old. If 2 compartments that do not face one another became damaged, such as the first and third, they are valid even if they are old. If 3 compartments became damaged, they are invalid in every case.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: Two courtyards that wish to make one eruv together, so as to permit even utensils that spent Shabbos in the houses, do not require a new eruv. Rather, one resident of the first courtyard may carry the eruv they already made on behalf of all of them and place it in one of the houses of the second courtyard. If he wishes, he may even bring bread of his own there, and all are permitted. {Rama: This applies provided that the residents of his own courtyard first joined in an eruv with him [Responsa of the Rosh, siman 16], or that they do not require an eruv, as explained in siman 370. [Beit Yosef]} This also requires that the residents of the second courtyard have made an eruv among themselves. They do not require additional bread; the eruv they already made permits them.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: If one placed a plank over the trench like a bridge, from one edge of the trench to the other, and it is 4 tefachim wide, it is considered an opening. The 2 courtyards may make one eruv together, or, if they wish, they may make 2 separate eruvin. {Rama: The same applies if one filled a width of 4 tefachim with material that he permanently leaves there. [Beit Yosef]} If the plank was laid lengthwise along the trench for a distance of 4 tefachim, then even if its width is only the smallest amount it is considered an opening, because it reduced the trench's width from 4 tefachim.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of washing the hands. It contains 23 seifim: One should wash his hands and recite the blessing over washing the hands. {Rama: Some say that he should also recite Asher Yatzar even if he did not relieve himself, and this is the custom. [Abudarham]} Water that is invalid for washing the hands for a meal, as discussed below in siman 160, is valid for washing the hands for prayer. However, some say that one does not recite a blessing over such water.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: One should not answer an Amen chatufah, meaning as though the alef were vocalized with a chataf, nor should he snatch and hurry to answer Amen before the one reciting the blessing has finished. He should also not answer an Amen ketufah, meaning that he omits the pronunciation of the nun and does not articulate it clearly. He should also not interrupt in the middle of the word. [Beit Yosef in the name of the Aruch] He should not answer an Amen yetomah, meaning that he is obligated in a certain blessing and the prayer leader is reciting it, but he does not hear the blessing. Even though he knows which blessing the prayer leader is reciting, since he did not hear it he should not answer Amen after him, for that is an Amen yetomah. {Rama: Some are stringent that even if one is not obligated in that blessing, he should not answer Amen if he does not know which blessing the prayer leader is reciting, for this too is called an Amen yetomah. [Tur in the name of Rashbatz] One should not delay answering Amen. Rather, immediately when the blessing concludes, he should answer Amen. [Abudarham]} One should not answer a short Amen, but should lengthen it somewhat, long enough to say 'El Melech Ne'eman.' He should not lengthen it excessively, because the word is no longer heard properly when it is prolonged too much.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The Kohanim stand on the platform with their faces toward the Ark and their backs toward the people, and their fingers bent into their palms, until the prayer leader finishes Modim. Then, if there are 2 Kohanim, the prayer leader calls out to them, 'Kohanim.' [Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah and Rambam] {Rama: He should not say 'Our God and God of our fathers,' etc. Some say that he recites it quietly until the word 'Kohanim,' and then says that word aloud. [Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah and Maharam of Rothenburg] He then returns and says 'Your holy people, as stated' quietly, and this is the custom in these lands.} They turn their faces toward the people. If there is only 1 Kohen, the prayer leader does not call him; rather, the Kohen turns his face on his own.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The Kohanim begin by saying 'Yevarechecha.' {Rama: Some say that the prayer leader should first call out even the word 'Yevarechecha' to them. [Tur, Ran in the chapter HaKoreh, and Hagahot Maimoniyot] This is the custom in all these lands.} Afterward, the prayer leader reads the blessing to them word by word, and they repeat each word after him until they finish the first verse, at which point the congregation answers Amen. The same procedure is followed after the second verse and after the third verse.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: Even the head of the congregation or the chazzan should not read from the Torah until he is told, 'Read.' The custom, however, is that when the prayer leader wishes, he recites the blessing and reads without first obtaining permission, because it is regarded as though, when he was appointed prayer leader, permission for this was already granted to him. {Rama: In these lands this is not the custom, and the chazzan goes up only when the gabbai tells him to go up. He is not called by name like other people receiving an aliyah, who are called 'so-and-so son of so-and-so.' One whose father became an apostate to idolatry is called by his grandfather's name, and not by his own name alone, so as not to shame him publicly. [Terumat HaDeshen, simanim 21 and 68] This applies when he had not previously been accustomed to be called by his father's name. But if he is an adult and was already accustomed in that city to be called by his father's name, and afterward his father became an apostate, he is called by his father's name as before, so as not to shame him publicly. The same applies where there is concern for hostility from the apostate. [Maharam Padua, siman 87] An asufi and a shetuki are called by the name of their maternal grandfather. If even that is unknown, they are called 'son of Avraham,' like a convert. [Rama's own ruling] Maharil wrote that nowadays a blind person may be called to the Torah just as an am ha'aretz may be called.} A blind person is forbidden to read from the Torah, because one may not read even one letter by heart.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: Raising and rubbing the hands when washing. It contains 10 seifim: One who washes his hands must raise them, meaning the tips of his fingers, upward, so that the water will not flow beyond the joint and then return and render the hands impure. {Rama: The same law applies if he keeps them lowered from the beginning of the washing until the end, which is also valid. He must only be careful not first to raise the fingertips and then lower them, because the water would then flow beyond the joint and return and render the hands impure. [Beit Yosef in the name of Mahari ibn Chaviv]} This applies when one does not wash the entire hand up to the place where the hand joins the arm. But if he washes up to there, he need not raise his hands. Some disagree. Likewise, if he poured a revi'it over both hands at once, since there is no impure water remaining, he need not raise his hands. One who immerses his hands likewise need not raise them. {Rama: Some say that if one pours 3 times, he need not be careful about all of this, and the custom is to be lenient. [Agur in the name of Or Zarua and Hagahot Ashiri]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: If one erred and did not mention Rosh Chodesh in Birkat HaMazon, whether by day or by night, he says, 'Blessed is He who gave New Moons to His people Israel as a remembrance,' and does not conclude it with a blessing formula, provided that he remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv. If he did not remember until after beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he does not return, because he is not obligated to eat bread on Rosh Chodesh in a manner that requires Birkat HaMazon. Chol HaMoed has the same law as Rosh Chodesh. If Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbos and he mentioned Shabbos but not Rosh Chodesh, and he did not remember until after beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he does not return. If he also forgot Shabbos and remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he combines Rosh Chodesh with Shabbos and says, 'Who gave Shabbosos for rest and New Moons for remembrance.' If he already began HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he returns to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon and mentions both Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh. Some say that if he forgot both Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh and remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he says, 'Who gave Shabbosos for rest and New Moons for remembrance,' and concludes with the concluding formula for Shabbos but not for Rosh Chodesh. {Rama: It is possible that he should nevertheless mention Rosh Chodesh among the other HaRachaman passages, as explained above at the end of siman 187 regarding Al HaNissim. Perhaps, however, there is a distinction, because Ya'aleh VeYavo contains Divine Names and one should not recite them in vain. So it appears to me, and this is the custom.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: That all one's intentions should be for the sake of Heaven. It contains 1 seif: If one cannot study without sleeping in the afternoon, he should sleep. {Rama: When he wakes from his sleep, he need not recite Elohai Neshamah. [Beit Yosef] Some say that before sleeping he should recite Vihi Noam. [Kol Bo]} He should not prolong his sleep, because one may not sleep during the day more than the sleep of a horse, which is 60 breaths. Even in this short sleep, his intention should not be for bodily pleasure, but to strengthen his body for the service of Hashem. Likewise, with everything from which he derives pleasure in this world, he should not intend his own pleasure but the service of the Creator, as it is written, 'In all your ways know Him,' and the Sages said, 'Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.' Even optional matters, such as eating, drinking, walking, sitting, standing, marital relations, conversation, and all bodily needs, should all be directed toward serving his Creator or toward something that enables His service. Thus, even if he is thirsty or hungry, if he eats or drinks for his own pleasure it is not praiseworthy. Rather, he should intend to eat and drink what is necessary for his vitality in order to serve his Creator. Likewise, even sitting among the upright, standing among the righteous, or walking in the counsel of the wholehearted is not praiseworthy if he does so for his own pleasure and to satisfy his desire, unless he acts for the sake of Heaven. The same applies to lying down. It goes without saying that when he can engage in Torah study or mitzvot, he should not entice himself with sleep for pleasure. Even when he is tired and needs sleep to rest from his fatigue, if he sleeps for bodily pleasure it is not praiseworthy. Rather, he should intend to give sleep to his eyes and rest to his body as required for health, so that his mind will not become confused in Torah study because of lack of sleep. Likewise regarding marital relations: even at the time required by the Torah, if he acts for bodily pleasure it is disgraceful. Even if his intention is to have children who will serve him and take his place, it is not praiseworthy. Rather, he should intend to have children who will serve his Creator, or intend to fulfill the prescribed mitzvah as one who pays a debt. Likewise regarding conversation: even when speaking words of wisdom, his intention must be for the service of the Creator or for something that leads to His service. The general principle is that a person must direct his eyes and heart to his ways and weigh all his deeds on the scales of reason. Whatever he sees will bring him to the service of the Creator, he should do, and whatever will not, he should not do. One who conducts himself in this manner serves his Creator constantly.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: The law of embarking on a ship and traveling with a caravan on Shabbos. It contains 4 seifim: It is permitted to embark on a ship even on Friday if one is traveling for the purpose of a mitzvah. He should stipulate with the non-Jew that the ship rest on Shabbos, and if afterward the non-Jew does not rest, it is of no consequence. For an optional journey, one may not embark within 3 days before Shabbos. If it is a short journey, such as from Tyre to Sidon, which can be completed in one day, it is permitted to embark on Friday morning because it is possible to reach the destination before Shabbos. In a place where the custom is not to embark at all on Friday, even for a short journey, it is forbidden. {Rama: More than 3 days before Shabbos it is permitted even on boats that are drawn by animals, and even where the water is less than 10 tefachim deep. [Maharik] This is so even if the Jew will afterward need to perform a melacha on Shabbos in order to direct the ship. [Rivash]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: It is forbidden on Friday to establish a meal and drinking feast that one is not accustomed to have on weekdays, even if it is an engagement meal, because of the honor of Shabbos, so that one will enter Shabbos with an appetite and eat the Shabbos meal with desire. This prohibition applies throughout the day. Eating and drinking without establishing a meal, and even eating a meal of the sort one ordinarily eats on a weekday, are permitted by the strict law throughout the day. Nevertheless, it is a mitzvah to refrain from establishing a meal from the ninth hour onward. {Rama: A mitzvah meal that occurs on Friday, such as a circumcision or pidyon haben, is permitted, as explained above, and this is the prevalent custom.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: One may say to another person on Shabbos, 'Tomorrow I am going to such-and-such a city,' and may likewise say, 'Come with me tomorrow to such-and-such a city,' since it would be possible to reach it today by means of huts extending the techum. The same applies to anything of this kind where there is some permitted way to do it today: one may tell another person to do it tomorrow, provided that he does not mention payment. But regarding something for which there is no permitted way to do it today, even if the prohibition is only rabbinic, such as fruit that is muktzeh and lies outside the techum, since it is impossible to bring it today, one may not tell another person to bring it for him tomorrow. He may likewise not wait at the end of the techum toward nightfall so that he can hurry there at night to bring it. {Rama: He should also not say, 'I will do such-and-such tomorrow.' [Rosh, chapter HaShoel; see above at the beginning of this siman]} He may, however, wait at the end of the techum toward nightfall in order to hurry there at night to guard the fruit, because even today he could guard it if it were within the techum. If his intention in waiting there was only to guard it, he may afterward also bring it.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama material restored in source order.

new_en: They shall be written in black ink, whether it contains gallnut water or does not contain gallnut water. {Rama: Ideally, one should be stringent to write with ink made from the soot of wood or oils soaked in gallnut water. [Maharil, siman 119] This is as will be explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 271.} If even 1 letter was written with another type of coloring substance or with gold, they are invalid. If gold dust was cast upon the letters, one removes the gold and the writing underneath remains, and it is valid. But if gold was cast upon a letter of a Divine Name, there is no remedy, because it is forbidden to remove the gold, since doing so is considered erasing the Divine Name.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of bathing on Shabbos. It contains 13 seifim: It is forbidden to wash one's entire body, even limb by limb separately, even with water that was heated before Shabbos, whether the water is in a vessel or in the ground. It is even forbidden to pour the water over one's body and wash. But one may wash his face, hands, and feet with it. {Rama: Or other limbs, provided that he does not wash his entire body. [Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh, chapter Tinokot]} These restrictions apply to water heated by fire. With the hot springs of Tiberias, however, it is permitted to wash even one's entire body at once, and certainly in cold water. The permission regarding the hot springs of Tiberias applies specifically when the water is in the ground, but not when it is in a vessel, lest it be confused with water heated by fire.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If a refuse heap in the public domain is 10 tefachim high and 4 tefachim wide, and it belongs to the public, one may throw into it from an adjacent private domain. {Rama: We are not concerned that the object might roll from the refuse heap into the public domain and that he may come to carry it, because people ordinarily throw only repulsive things onto a refuse heap. [Maggid Mishneh, chapter 15, in the name of Rashba]} If the refuse heap belongs to an individual, it is forbidden, because an individual is apt to clear away his refuse heap, and people will then continue pouring there in their usual manner and will thereby be pouring into the public domain.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of relinquishing domain by those who forgot to make an eruv. It contains 2 seifim: All the laws of relinquishing domain that apply to one who forgot and did not join the eruv in his courtyard likewise apply in an alleyway. Thus, if 1 courtyard forgot and did not participate in the shituf, it may relinquish its domain to the other residents of the alleyway, or they may relinquish theirs to it, even though they are many, because the residents of a courtyard are considered, relative to the alleyway, like a single individual in a courtyard. All the laws governing Jews in a courtyard together with a non-Jew likewise apply in an alleyway or city. Carrying is not prohibited in an alleyway or in a walled city until there are 2 courtyards containing Jewish houses in the city; 1 courtyard does not suffice, even if many Jewish houses open into it. This applies when the city was enclosed by a wall for residential purposes. Ordinary towns are presumed to have been enclosed for residential purposes, while ordinary fortresses are not. When there are 2 courtyards of Jewish houses in the city, the right of use must be rented from each courtyard of non-Jews, and it is not sufficient to rent from the city official. {Rama: Some say this distinction applies specifically to bringing objects into and out of the non-Jew's domain. For carrying in the alleyway, however, one may rent from the city official, since the roadway of the alleyway belongs to him and he has the power to remove all the non-Jews from there. [Rivash, siman 710] This applies to an official who does not own the houses and has no right at all to use the houses of the city's residents, even in wartime. But where all affairs of the city are conducted only through the official or his appointee, renting from that official or from his agent is sufficient, because he has the right in wartime to place his men and weapons in the residents' houses without their consent.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If a house is within 70 amot and a remainder of the city, and a second house is within 70 amot and a remainder of the first house, and a third house is within that distance of the second, and so on even for a journey of several days, all are considered 1 city. When measuring the techum, one measures from outside the last house, provided that this residential house is at least 4 amot by 4 amot. Likewise, a synagogue that contains a dwelling for its attendants, a house of idolatry that contains a dwelling for its priests, storehouses that contain a dwelling, a bridge or grave containing a dwelling, 3 walls without a roof that enclose an area of 4 by 4 amot, a house built in the sea, 2 walls with a roof and ceiling over them, and a cave with a structure over its entrance containing a dwelling, all join the city if they are within 70 amot and a remainder. From the outermost such house we regard it as though a line were stretched across the face of the entire city, and the 2,000 amot are measured outside that line. {Rama: If there are 2 such houses opposite the city, their law is like a city shaped as an arch. [Tur]} But 2 walls without a roof, even if people live between them; a bridge or grave; a synagogue, house of idolatry, or storehouse without a dwelling; a pit, cistern, cave, dovecote, or house on a ship, and the like, do not join the city.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: That an eruv techumin is made only for a mitzvah purpose. It contains 4 seifim: One may make an eruv techumin only for a mitzvah purpose, such as when he wishes to go to a house of mourning, to a wedding feast, to greet his rabbi, or to greet his friend who has returned from a journey, and similar purposes. {Rama: The same applies if he wishes to go for pleasure on Yom Tov or Shabbos to an orchard where this will bring him joy; this is considered a mitzvah purpose. [Terumat HaDeshen, siman 77]} The same applies because of fear, such as when he wishes to flee from non-Jews, robbers, or the like; in such a case he may then go even for an optional purpose. [Tur and Hagahot Ashiri, chapter Bechol Me'arvin] If he made an eruv for none of these purposes, but rather for an optional purpose, the eruv is nevertheless valid.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of the morning blessings and other blessings. It contains 9 seifim: When he awakens from his sleep he says Elohai Neshamah. When he hears the rooster's call he recites the blessing Hanoten LaSechvi Vinah. When he dresses he recites Malbish Arumim. When he passes his hands over his eyes he recites Pokeach Ivrim. When he sits up he recites Matir Asurim. When he straightens himself he recites Zokef Kefufim. When he places his feet on the ground he recites Roka HaAretz Al HaMayim. When he puts on his shoes he recites SheAsah Li Kol Tzorki. When he walks he recites HaMechin Mitzadei Gaver. When he girds his belt he recites Ozer Yisrael BiGevurah. {Rama: Or when he puts on the sash that separates between his heart and his ervah. [Beit Yosef in the name of Ra'avad]} When he places a hat or turban on his head he recites Oter Yisrael BeTifarah. When he washes his hands he recites Al Netilat Yadayim. When he washes his face he recites HaMa'avir Sheinah MeEinai, etc., and Yehi Ratzon, etc., through the conclusion, 'Blessed are You, Hashem, who bestows good kindnesses upon His people Israel.' One should not answer Amen after HaMa'avir Sheinah MeEinai until he concludes 'who bestows good kindnesses upon His people Israel,' because it is all 1 blessing.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: A plate is brought before the head of the household containing 3 matzot, maror, charoset, karpas or another vegetable, vinegar or salt water, and 2 cooked foods, 1 as a remembrance of the Pesach offering and 1 as a remembrance of the Chagigah offering. The custom is to use meat and an egg. {Rama: He should arrange the plate before himself so that he will not have to pass over any mitzvah. Thus, the karpas should be above everything, with the vinegar next to it and closer to him than the matzah; the matzot should be closer than the maror and charoset; and these should be closer to him than the meat and egg. [Maharil]} The custom is that the meat should be a foreleg, and that it should be roasted over coals. The egg should be cooked; the same applies if it is roasted, and that is the custom in our city.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: He washes his hands for the first dipping and does not recite a blessing over the washing. He takes less than a kezayit of karpas, dips it in vinegar, recites Borei Pri HaAdamah, and eats it, without reciting an after-blessing. He then takes the middle matzah and breaks it into 2. He gives half to 1 of those reclining at the table to keep for the afikoman, and they place it under the cloth. He places the other half between the 2 whole matzot. He lifts the plate containing the matzot and recites Ha Lachma Anya until Mah Nishtanah. {Rama: They should say it in a language understood by the women and children, or explain the matter to them. R' Yitzchak of London likewise recited the entire Haggadah in the vernacular so that the women and children would understand. [Kol Bo and Mahariv]} He then instructs that the matzot be removed from the table and placed at the far end of the table, as though they had already eaten, so that the children will see and ask.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Not to prepare on 1 Yom Tov for another day. It contains 2 seifim: It is forbidden to bake, cook, or slaughter on Yom Tov for the needs of the following day, even if the following day is Shabbos or Yom Tov, and even on the 2 days of Rosh Hashana. A woman may, however, fill a pot with meat even though she needs only 1 piece. {Rama: All the more so, one may slaughter even though he needs only a kezayit. [Semak] Likewise, she may cook many pots and eat a little from each. [Beit Yosef, Rabbeinu Yeruham, and a responsum of Rashba] This applies specifically before eating. After she has eaten, however, she may not cook and say that she will eat a kezayit from it, because that is a ruse. Nevertheless, if she transgressed and cooked, or slaughtered, it is permitted to eat it.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The law of items brought on Yom Tov from outside the techum. It contains 9 seifim: If a non-Jew brings a gift to a Jew on Yom Tov, and items of that species are still attached to the ground or require trapping, it is forbidden even for a person for whom they were not brought to eat them that day. Even if he transgressed and put one in his mouth and chewed it, he may not swallow it. [R' Shimshon in his commentary to the Mishnah, chapter 2 of Terumot] It is even forbidden to move them. In the evening they become permitted after the amount of time required to perform the act has elapsed. On the 2 Yom Tov days observed in the Diaspora, if they were brought on the first day, they are permitted on the night of the second Yom Tov after the required amount of time has elapsed. {Rama: Some are stringent and forbid them until after the second Yom Tov. [Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, Rashi, and Semag] The custom is to be stringent when they are not needed for Yom Tov itself. For guests and similar needs, however, the custom is to be lenient for people for whom they were not brought. [Terumat HaDeshen, siman 78]} Likewise, if they were brought on the second Yom Tov, one must wait after Yom Tov for the required amount of time. But on the 2 days of Rosh Hashana, or when Yom Tov adjoins Shabbos either before it or after it, if they were brought on the first day, one must wait until after Yom Tov and Shabbos and then the required amount of time. The required amount of time is enough time for the non-Jew to go to the place where he gathered them, complete the melacha, and return here. If there is uncertainty as to where they were brought from, the required time is the amount needed for them to have been brought from outside the techum.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of rejoicing on Yom Tov. It contains 4 seifim: The mitzvah of Yom Tov is to divide it, half for the beit midrash and half for eating and drinking. One should not be sparing with Yom Tov expenses, and one must honor and enjoy it as on Shabbos. {Rama: It is forbidden to eat from Minchah onward on the eve of Yom Tov, as on the eve of Shabbos, because this is part of honoring the day. [Rambam, chapter 6] However, if the eve of Yom Tov is Shabbos, he may fulfill seudah shlishit, but should eat only a little bread in honor of Yom Tov. It is a mitzvah to knead bread on the eve of Yom Tov in honor of Yom Tov, as on the eve of Shabbos, as explained above in siman 242. [Maharil, Laws of Yom Tov]} One is obligated to break bread over 2 loaves and to establish every meal over wine. Yom Tov clothing should be finer than Shabbos clothing. The custom is not to eat seudah shlishit on Yom Tov. On Yom Tov they come later to the synagogue and leave earlier because of the rejoicing of Yom Tov. [Gemara, chapter HaKoreh Omed]
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If one erred and said, 'who by His word brings on evenings,' then immediately remembered and said, 'who forms light,' and also concluded, 'who forms the luminaries,' he has fulfilled his obligation. But if he said, 'who by His word brings on evenings,' and did not say, 'who forms light,' or did not conclude, 'who forms the luminaries,' he has not fulfilled his obligation. If he said, 'who forms light and creates darkness, who by His word brings on evenings,' and also concluded, 'who brings on evenings,' he has not fulfilled his obligation. {Rama: The same applies if at the beginning he said only, 'who forms light': if he concluded, 'who brings on evenings,' he has not fulfilled his obligation. [Rama's own ruling, explaining the Tur and Rosh]} But if he concluded, 'who forms the luminaries,' then since he began with 'who forms light,' he has fulfilled his obligation even though he interrupted with the words concerning bringing on evenings.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The blessing Yotzer and the evening blessing should be recited quietly together with the prayer leader. {Rama: One should hasten to finish before the prayer leader finishes and answer Amen after the prayer leader. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 1 of the Laws of Blessings, and Rokeach, siman 218] Nevertheless, if he did not recite the blessing himself but only heard it from the prayer leader, he has fulfilled his obligation, because for these blessings the prayer leader can discharge the obligation of an individual even if that person is proficient. The prayer leader cannot, however, discharge an individual's obligation with fewer than 10 present. [Rabbeinu Yonah, chapter Mi SheMeito]} One should not answer Amen after the conclusion 'who chooses His people Israel with love,' because that would constitute an interruption. See below, siman 61.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: One who makes a sukkah under a tree or under a roof. It contains 3 seifim: One should not make a sukkah beneath a house or a tree. One who makes his sukkah beneath a tree: some say that if the tree's shade exceeds its sunlight, the sukkah is invalid in every case, even if the sukkah itself has more shade than sunlight. But if the tree has more sunlight than shade, and the sukkah has more shade than sunlight without the tree, it is valid even if he did not lower the branches to mix them with the sukkah's schach. If, however, the sukkah has more shade than sunlight only because of the tree, he must lower the branches and mix them with the schach so that they are not distinguishable, with the valid schach exceeding and nullifying them. Others say that even when the sukkah has more shade than sunlight without the tree, and the tree has more sunlight than shade, if the tree branches are directly aligned above the valid schach the sukkah is invalid, whether the tree preceded the sukkah or the sukkah preceded the tree. {Rama: Nevertheless, if he lowers the branches and mixes them with the schach so that they are not distinguishable, they are nullified and the sukkah is valid. [Rosh and Ran] Likewise, if he placed valid schach upon the invalid schach, this is considered mixing and it is valid. [Mordechai, chapter 1 of Sukkah]} But if the branches are above the empty spaces between the valid schach, or there is so much valid schach that even if the amount corresponding to the tree were removed a valid measure would remain, the sukkah is valid, since the shade from valid schach still exceeds its sunlight. In all of this there is no distinction whether the tree preceded the schach or the schach preceded the tree; their law is the same.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The law of sitting during the recitation of Shema and not sleeping. It contains 9 seifim: One may recite it while walking, standing, lying down, riding upon an animal, or sitting, but not while lying face down or flat on his back with his face upward. He may recite while lying on his side. {Rama: This applies when he is already lying down and it would be burdensome to stand. [Rabbeinu Yonah, chapter Mi SheMeito]} If he is very heavy and cannot turn onto his side, or if he is ill, he should incline himself slightly to the side and recite it.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: If it was given to him without any explicit condition, it is as though the giver said, 'On condition that you return it to me,' because it is presumed that he gave it with that intention, since he himself needs it to fulfill the mitzvah and has no other. If the recipient did not return it, he did not fulfill the mitzvah. {Rama: He must give it back to its owner as a gift, so that it again belongs to the owner and the owner can fulfill the mitzvah with it. [Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruham, netiv 8, part 4]} Nevertheless, even if he did not return it directly to the owner's hand but gave it to another person, who gave it to another, and the last person returned it to the owner, he has fulfilled his obligation.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The order of circling the bimah. It contains 3 seifim: The custom is to bring a Sefer Torah to the bimah and circle it once each day, while on the seventh day they circle it 7 times, in remembrance of the Temple. {Rama: On the seventh day, 7 Sifrei Torah are brought to the bimah. [Maharil] In some places they bring out all the Sifrei Torah in the ark, and this is the custom in these lands. [Minhagim]} In the Temple they would circle the altar, and the circles are made toward the right. On Shabbos they do not circle. [Tur] One who has no lulav does not circle, and the same applies to one who is in mourning, according to the customs cited by the authorities.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The order of the Torah reading on Chol HaMoed. It contains 3 seifim: On Chol HaMoed of Sukkot, 4 people read the passages of the festival offerings in Parashat Pinchas. In the Diaspora, because of the uncertainty regarding the calendar day, the readings include the offerings of the 2 possible days. {Rama: Some say that the first 2 readers read the 2 doubtful-day portions, the third reads the offering of the following day, and the fourth returns and reads the 2 doubtful-day portions read by the first 2 readers, and this is our custom.} On the seventh day, the first reader reads 'On the fifth day,' the second 'On the sixth day,' the third 'On the seventh day,' and the fourth reads 'On the sixth day' and 'On the seventh day.' This is our custom. [Rashi in the name of his teachers; Mahariv; Minhagim] In Eretz Yisrael, where there is no uncertainty as to the day, the offering of that day is read.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of the sukkah on the seventh day. It contains 1 seif: Even if one finished eating on the morning of the seventh day, he should not dismantle his sukkah. From Minchah onward, however, he removes his utensils from it and prepares his house for the final Yom Tov. If he has no place to bring the utensils and wishes to continue eating in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret, he should reduce 4 by 4 tefachim of the schach, to make it evident that he is not sitting there for the mitzvah of sukkah and so that it should not appear that he is adding to the mitzvah. If he still needs to eat during the seventh day, he must eat in the sukkah, because its mitzvah applies throughout all 7 days. In the Diaspora, where one must sit in the sukkah also on Shemini Atzeret because of the doubt, when he finishes eating on Shemini Atzeret he removes the utensils. If he has nowhere to remove them and wishes to eat there on the ninth day, he cannot reduce the schach because it is Yom Tov. What should he do to distinguish his sitting from fulfillment of the mitzvah? If the sukkah is small enough that placing a lamp there was forbidden during Sukkot, he brings a lamp into it; if it is large enough that a lamp was permitted, he brings pots and similar utensils into it, demonstrating that its mitzvah has ended. {Rama: If he wishes to sit in the sukkah after Yom Tov, he need not reduce it, because the appearance of adding to the mitzvah applies only on Shemini Atzeret. [Minhagim]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The order of the prayer on the night and day of Shemini Atzeret. It contains 2 seifim: On the night of Shemini Atzeret one says in the prayer, 'And You gave us this eighth day, the festival of Atzeret.' {Rama: Our custom is not to say the word 'festival' regarding Shemini Atzeret, because we do not find it called a festival anywhere; rather, we say, 'the day of Shemini Atzeret.' [Minhagim]} In the Diaspora, one eats in the sukkah both at night and by day because of the doubt, but does not recite the blessing over sitting in the sukkah. Afterward, on the ninth day, one does not sit in the sukkah.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: We read the offerings of the nesi'im in Parashat Nasso, 3 readers each day. We begin with Birkat Kohanim. {Rama: Some say that we begin with 'And it was on the day that Moshe finished setting up the Mishkan,' and this is our custom. [Tur]} On the first day, the Kohen and Levi read from Birkat Kohanim, and the Yisrael reads the offering of the first day. {Rama: Some say that the Kohen reads the entire passage through 'on the first day,' and the Levi and Yisrael read the offering of the first day, and this is our custom.} On the second day, the Kohen reads from 'On the second day' through '1 young bull,' the Levi reads through 'On the third day,' and the Yisrael repeats from 'On the second day.' The same pattern is followed each day. {Rama: Some say that the Yisrael reads the offering of the following day, meaning on the second day he reads from 'On the third day,' and similarly on each day, and this is our custom. [Hagahot Maimoniyot]} On the eighth day we begin with 'On the eighth day,' complete the entire section, and read the beginning of Beha'alotcha. {Rama: Our custom is to conclude with 'So he made the menorah.' [Minhagim]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The Megillah must be read in its entirety and from the written text. If one read it by heart, he has not fulfilled his obligation. Ideally, the entire Megillah must be written before him. After the fact, however, if the scribe omitted words in its middle, even up to half of it, and the reader recited those words by heart, he has fulfilled his obligation. {Rama: But if the scribe omitted even a minority at its beginning or end, he has not fulfilled his obligation. [Ran] Even in the middle, this allowance applies only if an entire subject was not omitted. [Beit Yosef in the name of Orchot Chaim]} If more than half is missing, or even if it is written but blurred so that the writing is not discernible, the Megillah is invalid.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: One who is bathing naked in clear water and wishes to drink should cover himself with a garment from below his heart, so that his heart will not see his ervah when he recites the blessing. This specifically requires a garment; covering with the hands is not considered a covering. {Rama: The same applies if he covers his head with his hands; this is not considered a covering.} But if his heart is beneath the water while his ervah is also beneath the water, some authorities permit him to recite the blessing, while others require a separation between his heart and his ervah. If the water is cloudy so that his ervah cannot be seen through it, it is considered a covering.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Whether it is permitted to recite sacred texts in a bathhouse. It contains 1 seif: In a new bathhouse in which no one has yet bathed, it is permitted to recite sacred texts. In an old bathhouse, in the outer room where everyone present is clothed, it is permitted. In the middle room, where some are clothed and some are naked, one may exchange a greeting of Shalom, but may not recite Shema or pray. {Rama: It is permitted to think words of Torah there. [Ran, chapter 1 of Shabbos and chapter Kol HaTzelamim]} In the inner room, where everyone stands naked, even a greeting of Shalom is forbidden. It is also forbidden to answer Amen in a bathhouse. [Ran, chapter Kirah]
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.
